content: Industrial microbiology, also known as microbial biotechnology, involves the application of microorganisms in the production of food and industrial products. When microorganisms are used to produce food for humans or animals, this is often categorized under food microbiology. The microorganisms utilized in these processes can be naturally occurring strains, mutants selected in laboratories, or genetically modified organisms. In the realm of food microbiology, a wide array of products such as yogurt, cheese, chocolate, butter, pickles, sauerkraut, soy sauce, vitamins, amino acids, microbial polysaccharides (used as food thickeners), alcohol, sausages, and silage (animal feed) are manufactured through industrial microbiology techniques. Beneficial bacteria, such as probiotics, are gaining significant importance in the food industry due to their health-promoting properties. Microorganisms are also employed in the production of biopolymers, which include polysaccharides, polyesters, and polyamides. These biopolymers can range from viscous solutions to materials resembling plastics. Advances in genetic engineering have enabled the production of biopolymers with specific material properties, making them suitable for high-value medical applications such as tissue engineering and drug delivery systems. Examples of biopolymers synthesized through industrial microbiology include xanthan, alginate, cellulose, cyanophycin, poly(gamma-glutamic acid), levan, hyaluronic acid, organic acids, oligosaccharides, polysaccharides, and polyhydroxyalkanoates. Microbial biodegradation plays a critical role in bioremediation, which involves the cleanup of polluted environments. This process utilizes naturally occurring microorganisms to degrade, transform, or accumulate a wide range of pollutants, including hydrocarbons (e.g., oil), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), pharmaceutical compounds, radionuclides, and metals. In waste management, microorganisms are employed to treat the large volumes of waste generated by modern societies. Biotreatment, which involves the use of living organisms to process waste, is an environmentally sustainable, straightforward, and cost-effective alternative to traditional physical or chemical cleanup methods. These processes can be carried out in controlled environments such as bioreactors. In healthcare and medicine, microorganisms are utilized to produce biologics for humans and animals, including insulin, growth hormones, and antibodies. Additionally, diagnostic tools such as monoclonal antibody-based assays, DNA probe technologies, and real-time PCR are used in clinical laboratories for the rapid detection of pathogenic organisms. The study of extremophilic microorganisms, such as archaea that thrive in extreme environments (e.g., high temperatures, high salinity, low pH, or high radiation), has the potential to uncover novel microbial capabilities that can be applied in industrial processes. Corynebacteria represent a diverse group of Gram-positive bacteria found in various ecological niches, including soil, vegetables, sewage, human skin, and cheese surfaces. Among them, Corynebacterium glutamicum holds immense industrial significance. It is one of the most biotechnologically important bacterial species, with an annual production exceeding two million tons of amino acids, primarily L-glutamate and L-lysine. The genome of C. glutamicum has been sequenced, further enhancing its utility in industrial applications.
